Abstract

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Introduction
Physics contributed to the birth of knot theory in the 19th century, when Lord Kelvin hypothesized that
atoms are knotted vortices of aether [1]. Although the idea was doomed to fail,1 it is said to inspire the
first knot classification by Peter Guthrie Tait. Tait’s knot table had significant impact on developing
knot theory as a branch of pure mathematics, a subfield of topology. Until late 20th century advances in
knot theory were predominantly limited to math.

like to have more information about the system. In particular, one may be interested in quantifying the

blocks.title: Entropy of Entanglement
blocks.content:
Entropy of Entanglement
So far we avoided working with a precise quantitative measure of entanglement. In this section we will
discuss the von Neumann entropy, which provides one of the most common measures, and try to explain
why it is natural for the topological formulation of quantum mechanics.
The von Neumann, or entanglement entropy is defined in terms of density matrices. If a state is
pure, that is we have complete access to the information about it, encapsulated in a vector |Ψ⟩, then the
density matrix associated with the state is given by the “square” of the state vector:
ρ = |Ψ⟩⟨Ψ| .

Outlook
Hopefully the present notes convincingly demonstrate the potential and functionality of topology and, in
particular, knot theory in the discussion of quantum mechanics. We have shown that states and operators
can be thought as of topological spaces, equipped with a set of basic operations, such as braiding. The

blocks.title: Multipartite Entanglement
blocks.content:
Multipartite Entanglement
In section 4.2 we reviewed classification of bipartite entanglement and showed that a classification similar
to SLOCC is possible in terms of the number of connections (Wilson lines) held by the two subsystems.
How does this classification works for multipartite systems?
For a 3-qubit system the SLOCC classification expects four distinct classes, two of which are bisep-
arable (either all three qubits are separable, or two of them in the Bell-type entanglement). The other
two classes correspond to genuinely tripartite entanglement: the GHZ class and the W class [95].

blocks.title: Quantum Gravity
blocks.content:
Quantum Gravity
Knot theory explicitly appears in the construction of states of loop quantum gravity [101,110]. Quantum
states in this theory are similar to the Chern-Simons states used in this review, although they are based
on closed lines, or closed networks, which are analogs of conformal blocks mentioned here, but with no
open ends. Consequently, some questions addressed in this review, such as properties of multipartite
entanglement, can be studied in the context of loop quantum gravity, using similar techniques. See [111]
for a recent example.
